examples.sentence: Muscle mass tends to fall by roughly 3–8% per decade after about age 30 (Volpi et al., 2004), so the same BMI can mean more fat later in life.
BMI doesn’t measure body fat, and because muscle mass tends to decline with age (Volpi et al., 2004), an older adult can carry more fat at the same BMI.
Starting around age 30, adults lose an estimated 3–8% of their muscle mass per decade, and the rate is higher after age 60 (Volpi et al., 2004).
Age is another: muscle mass tends to fall by roughly 3–8% per decade after about age 30 (Volpi et al., 2004), so an older adult can have a “healthy” BMI with more fat and less muscle than before.
After age 30, adults lose an estimated 3–8% of muscle mass per decade, a process called sarcopenia (Volpi et al., 2004).
Sarcopenia: age-related muscle loss, estimated at about 3–8% of muscle mass per decade after age 30 (Volpi et al., 2004)
From Quetelet’s 1830s index to Ancel Keys naming it BMI in 1972 and the WHO categories.
BMI was created by Adolphe Quetelet in the 1830s, named by Ancel Keys in 1972
Ancel Keys (1972)
The term “Body Mass Index” was coined by American physiologist Ancel Keys in a 1972 paper published in the Journal of Chronic Diseases.
Ancel Keys and the Term "BMI" (1972)
1972: American physiologist Ancel Keys coined the term "Body Mass Index" in a landmark study
Ancel Keys and the Birth of "Body Mass Index" (1972)
In 1972, Keys and his colleagues published a landmark paper in the Journal of Chronic Diseases titled "Indices of relative weight and obesity.
The term "Body Mass Index" (BMI) was coined 140 years later by American physiologist Ancel Keys in a 1972 paper published in the Journal of Chronic Diseases.
From Adolphe Quetelet's 1832 formula to Ancel Keys naming it in 1972, WHO adoption, and modern critiques.
BMI entered medicine later: Ancel Keys named it in 1972, and NIH and WHO guidelines adopted it in the 1980s and 1990s (see our BMI history).
Adolphe Quetelet (1830s)
The formula was invented by Belgian mathematician and astronomer Adolphe Quetelet between 1830 and 1850.
Body Mass Index was invented in the 1830s by Belgian mathematician Adolphe Quetelet - notably, not a physician.
Overweight (BMI 25–29.9): hazard ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.91–0.96), ~6% lower all-cause mortality
Grade 2+ obesity (BMI ≥35): hazard ratio 1.29 (95% CI 1.18–1.41), ~29% higher mortality
All-cause mortality by BMI category (pooled adults, Flegal 2013)
Data: Flegal KM et al., JAMA 2013 (all adult ages pooled, 97 studies, ~2.88M individuals).
An observational finding: in some large cohort studies, people classed as overweight had similar or slightly lower all-cause mortality than those in the healthy range (Flegal et al., JAMA 2013).

In a pooled analysis of 97 studies, all-cause mortality in the overweight range was about 6% lower than in the healthy range (hazard ratio 0.94; Flegal et al., JAMA 2013); why is still argued over, and it is not a reason to aim for a higher BMI.

In a pooled analysis of 97 studies covering about 2.88 million people, all-cause mortality was about 29% higher at a BMI of 35 or more than in the healthy range (hazard ratio 1.29; Flegal et al., JAMA 2013).

The 29% higher all-cause mortality reported for BMI 35 and above in the pooled analysis includes this class (Flegal et al., JAMA 2013); the risks listed for classes I and II apply here at their highest.
At the NFL Scouting Combine, for example, 53.4% of prospects had a BMI of 30 or more, but only 8.9% had obesity by measured body fat (Provencher et al., 2018).
At the NFL Scouting Combine, 53.4% of prospects had a BMI of 30 or more, but only 8.9% had obesity when their body fat was measured.
BMI put 53.4% of prospects in the obesity range; measured body fat put 8.9% there (J Strength Cond Res 2018).

It can’t tell muscle from fat, so muscular athletes are frequently classed as overweight or obese with low body fat; at the NFL Combine, 53.4% had a BMI of 30+, but 8.9% had obesity by measured body fat.
Why BMI misclassifies muscular athletes: 53.4% of NFL prospects had a BMI of 30+, but 8.9% had obesity by body fat.

Your waist divided by your height: the 0.5 boundary and how it compares with BMI.
Waist-to-height ratio compares waist size to height and uses a universal 0.5 cutoff for everyone.
Waist-to-height ratio: Should be < 0.5 for optimal health
A healthy waist-to-height ratio is below 0.5 for both men and women.

Adults aged 18–60 should sleep at least 7 hours a night, according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society (CDC).

The World Health Organization established the current BMI classification system in 1995, defining underweight (below 18.5), normal weight (18.5–24.9), overweight (25–29.9), and obese (30+).

items.sentence: Unlike standard BMI, which only considers height and weight, lean body mass separates your weight into two meaningful components: fat mass and everything else.
items.heading: Lean Body Mass Calculator

items.sentence: This distinction is critical because two people can weigh the same yet have vastly different health profiles.
items.heading: Lean Body Mass Calculator

items.sentence: Body composition is one of the health-related components of physical fitness, alongside cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance and flexibility (Caspersen et al., Public Health Reports 1985).
items.heading: Lean Body Mass Calculator

items.sentence: This calculator uses the Boer formula (published by P. Boer in 1984) to estimate lean body mass.
items.heading: The Boer Formula Explained

items.sentence: Boer developed it to normalise body fluid volumes, as the title of his 1984 paper says.
items.heading: The Boer Formula Explained
